lesson.title: Letting Boolean Expressions Steer the Program
lesson.summary: A conditional statement uses the truth value of a boolean expression to decide, at the moment the program runs, which block of code actually executes, connecting the logic you write to the control flow the computer follows.
lesson.body:
A conditional statement is the mechanism that turns a boolean expression into a decision about control flow. Everything covered so far, the boolean type, the logical operators and, or, and not, comparisons, operator precedence, and how they combine, exists to produce a single True or False value. A conditional statement is what actually does something with that value: it tells Python "if this expression is True, run this block of code, and otherwise, do not." Without conditionals, a boolean expression is just an interesting fact about your data; with them, it becomes a fork in the road the program actually takes.

In Python, every conditional statement follows the same structural pattern: a keyword (if, elif, or the case clauses inside match), a boolean expression, a colon, and an indented block that only runs when the expression is True. That indentation is doing real work, it is how Python knows where the conditional block ends and the surrounding sequential code resumes. This is why conditional statements are described as built on control flow generally, they are one specific, concrete way of choosing which statement runs next, layered on top of boolean expressions specifically, which supply the yes-or-no answer the choice depends on.

Trace a minimal example: age = 20, followed by if age >= 18 and has_id:, followed by an indented print("Entry allowed"). Python evaluates the boolean expression first, completely, before deciding anything about control flow. Suppose has_id is True. Then age >= 18 evaluates to True, since 20 is at least 18, and True and True evaluates to True. Because the overall expression is True, Python executes the indented block and prints "Entry allowed". If has_id had instead been False, the expression would evaluate to False regardless of age, the indented block would be skipped entirely, and execution would resume at whatever statement follows the conditional at the original indentation level.

It is worth being precise about what "conditional statement" refers to as an umbrella term. If, if-else, elif chains, and the match statement are all different syntactic shapes for the same underlying idea: choose a path based on a boolean expression, or in the case of match, based on whether a value matches a pattern. Nested conditionals combine several of these shapes inside one another for more complex decisions, and the ternary expression squeezes a small if-else into a single expression rather than a full statement. Every one of those specific tools is a variation on the general concept introduced here.

The practical value of conditional statements is that they let a single piece of code behave differently depending on the data it receives, without you having to write a separate program for every possible input. A single well-written conditional, backed by a correctly reasoned boolean expression, can replace what would otherwise require an entirely different sequence of statements for every case you care about.
